model_blind_spots: Two factors the model cannot fully capture could matter most for you: pension and income splitting between spouses, which could shift the household tax picture, and future legislative changes to the government programs that form your entire income floor. couple_analysis: As a couple, the order in which you draw from accounts and how you share income across two tax returns shape how long the savings stretch and how much tax the household pays. If you, the primary holder, were to die first, your partner would keep their own pensions plus a survivor Canada Pension Plan benefit, and the tax-free account would transfer with no tax, though total household income would step down. If your partner were to die first, you would retain all the registered accounts, with the partner's savings staying within the household. Either path would change the income mix, which is why coordinating withdrawals now matters for both futures.
spending_flex: Your spending is set as fixed, which means the portfolio absorbs the full force of market swings without any built-in cushion from reduced draws. In a stretch of weak returns, that rigidity could pull the balance down faster, since the same dollars come out regardless of how the markets behave. Even a small willingness to trim draws in down years could meaningfully lengthen how long the savings last.
sequence_risk: The portfolio outcomes spread from a cautious balance on the lower end to a far more favorable one on the upper end, and much of that gap comes down to the order in which returns arrive. Two identical portfolios can end up far apart when one meets weak markets early in retirement while still drawing income, because losses taken near the start are the hardest to recover from.
